lead: A Merkle tree takes many transaction hashes, pairs them, hashes each pair, and repeats until one hash remains: the Merkle root. A block header stores that one root, so 32 bytes stand for thousands of transactions. The tree also makes proof cheap: to show that one transaction is in the block, you send only the sibling hashes on its path to the root, about log₂ n hashes. Bitcoin uses this design; Ethereum uses a Merkle Patricia trie. The build, the proof and the common mistakes follow.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for the hash function H and collision resistance, and Chapter 2.3 for why a block header carries one root hash.

blocks.text: Start with n transactions T<sub>1</sub> … T<sub>n</sub>. Each transaction is hashed once: h<sub>i</sub> = H(T<sub>i</sub>). These hashes are the leaves. A leaf is a node with no children. The tree is binary: each internal node has two children. An internal node stores the hash of its two child hashes joined in order: H(left || right). The two vertical bars || mean concatenation: write the left hash bytes, then the right hash bytes.

Pair leaves from left to right: h<sub>1</sub> with h<sub>2</sub>, h<sub>3</sub> with h<sub>4</sub>, and so on. Hash each pair to get the next level. Repeat on that level. Stop when one hash remains. That top hash is the Merkle root R. It is also called the root hash.

items: Hash every transaction: h<sub>i</sub> = H(T<sub>i</sub>). These are the leaves.
Join neighbours in order: h<sub>12</sub> = H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>), h<sub>34</sub> = H(h<sub>3</sub> || h<sub>4</sub>), and so on.
Repeat on the new level until one hash is left. That hash is R.
If a level has an odd count, duplicate the last hash and pair it with itself. Bitcoin does this.

blocks.text: R = H( H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>) || H(h<sub>3</sub> || h<sub>4</sub>) )
blocks.where: H is the hash function (SHA-256 in Bitcoin); || joins two hashes in fixed left-to-right order; h<sub>1</sub> = H(T<sub>1</sub>) and so on; R is the Merkle root, 32 bytes for SHA-256.

blocks.text: For four transactions the height is two hash steps above the leaves. A tree with n leaves has about log₂ n levels, because each level halves the node count.

A Merkle path, also called a Merkle proof or inclusion proof, shows that one transaction is in the tree. The verifier already trusts the root R from the block header. The prover sends the transaction and the sibling hash at each level, from the leaf upward. The verifier hashes the transaction to get its leaf, joins it with the first sibling in the correct order, hashes, and repeats. If the final hash equals R, the transaction is included.

Order matters. At each step the verifier must know whether the running hash is the left child or the right child. A proof therefore carries a side bit, or the verifier knows the index of the transaction in the block. Swapping the two inputs gives a different hash and the check fails.

For n leaves the path has about log₂ n hashes; exactly, at most ceil(log₂ n). A block with 1,024 transactions needs at most 10 hashes, not 1,024. That is the reason the tree exists. Payment verification with such proofs is covered in Unit 4, Bitcoin and Cryptocurrencies.

Odd levels need care. If a level has an odd number of nodes, Bitcoin copies the last node and hashes it with itself: H(x || x). The copy is not stored as a new transaction; it is a rule for building the level. A proof for that last node includes x as its own sibling.

The Merkle root is a commitment. Change one transaction, and its leaf hash changes. That changes every hash on the path to the root. The root changes. Because the block header holds the root and the header is itself hashed into the next block (see Chapter 2.3), an edit cannot hide.

The root does not prove that a transaction is valid, that it has a signature, or that it is not a double spend. It proves only that the transaction is in the set committed by that root. Validation is separate: signatures are in Chapter 2.6; the transaction life cycle is in Unit 3.

Bitcoin uses a binary Merkle tree over transaction IDs. Ethereum uses a different structure, a Merkle Patricia trie, for accounts and storage; the name is enough here. Some syllabi call this topic digital structures in blockchain. The main exam skill is to build the levels, recompute the path after one change, and state the size of a proof.

figure.caption: T3 is the highlighted leaf. To prove it, send siblings h4 and h12: compute h34 = H(h3 || h4), then R = H(h12 || h34).

spec.aria: A four-leaf Merkle tree: h1 and h2 give h12, h3 and h4 give h34, and h12 and h34 give the Merkle root R. The proof for T3 highlights h3 and its sibling hashes h4 and h12.

examples.question: Four transactions T<sub>1</sub>, T<sub>2</sub>, T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub> have hashes h<sub>1</sub> = H(T<sub>1</sub>), h<sub>2</sub> = H(T<sub>2</sub>), h<sub>3</sub> = H(T<sub>3</sub>) and h<sub>4</sub> = H(T<sub>4</sub>). (a) Write the Merkle root R. (b) Transaction T<sub>3</sub> is replaced by T<sub>3</sub>′. Which stored hashes must be recomputed, and what is the new root?
steps: Pair the leaves in order: h<sub>12</sub> = H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>) and h<sub>34</sub> = H(h<sub>3</sub> || h<sub>4</sub>).
Hash the two level-1 hashes in order: R = H(h<sub>12</sub> || h<sub>34</sub>) = H( H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>) || H(h<sub>3</sub> || h<sub>4</sub>) ).
For the change, compute the new leaf h<sub>3</sub>′ = H(T<sub>3</sub>′). h<sub>1</sub>, h<sub>2</sub> and h<sub>4</sub> do not change.
Recompute the parent of h<sub>3</sub>′ and h<sub>4</sub>: h<sub>34</sub>′ = H(h<sub>3</sub>′ || h<sub>4</sub>). The other parent h<sub>12</sub> = H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>) does not change.
Recompute the root: R′ = H(h<sub>12</sub> || h<sub>34</sub>′). Only h<sub>3</sub>′, h<sub>34</sub>′ and R′ are new; h<sub>12</sub> is reused.
examples.answer: R = H( H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>) || H(h<sub>3</sub> || h<sub>4</sub>) ); after T<sub>3</sub> changes, recompute h<sub>3</sub>′, h<sub>34</sub>′ and R′, while h<sub>12</sub> stays the same.

traps: Reversing the pair: H(h<sub>2</sub> || h<sub>1</sub>) is not H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>). A proof must keep left and right.
Odd level: forget to duplicate the last hash, or duplicate a middle hash. Bitcoin duplicates only the last node at that level.
Mixing raw data and hashes: internal nodes hash two hashes, not two raw transactions.
Confusing the Merkle root with the block hash. The root covers transactions; the block hash covers the header.
Saying a proof needs all transactions or n hashes. It needs about log₂ n sibling hashes.

quiz.q: Define leaf, internal node and Merkle root in a Merkle tree.
quiz.a: A leaf is a node with no children, here h<sub>i</sub> = H(T<sub>i</sub>). An internal node hashes its two child hashes in order. The Merkle root is the single top hash.

quiz.q: Why does a block header store the Merkle root instead of every transaction hash?
quiz.a: One 32-byte root commits to all transactions and fits in the fixed header; changing any transaction changes the root. It also makes short inclusion proofs possible.

quiz.q: A block has 64 transactions. What is the maximum number of hashes in a Merkle proof for one transaction?
quiz.a: ceil(log₂ 64) = 6 hashes. The verifier also needs the transaction itself and the side bits.

quiz.q: Five leaves h<sub>1</sub> … h<sub>5</sub>. Write the level-1 hashes and the root using Bitcoin's odd rule.
quiz.a: Level 1: h<sub>12</sub> = H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>), h<sub>34</sub> = H(h<sub>3</sub> || h<sub>4</sub>), h<sub>55</sub> = H(h<sub>5</sub> || h<sub>5</sub>). Level 2: h<sub>1234</sub> = H(h<sub>12</sub> || h<sub>34</sub>), h<sub>5555</sub> = H(h<sub>55</sub> || h<sub>55</sub>). Root R = H(h<sub>1234</sub> || h<sub>5555</sub>).

quiz.q: If T<sub>2</sub> changes in the four-transaction tree, list the stored hashes that must be recomputed.
quiz.a: h<sub>2</sub>′ = H(T<sub>2</sub>), h<sub>12</sub>′ = H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>′), R′ = H(h<sub>12</sub>′ || h<sub>34</sub>). h<sub>1</sub>, h<sub>3</sub>, h<sub>4</sub> and h<sub>34</sub> stay the same.

quiz.q: A verifier receives a transaction, a Merkle path and a root. State two checks the path does not perform and why.
quiz.a: It does not check the transaction signature or that the transaction is spendable; those need public-key checks and ledger rules. It only checks membership under the root.

quiz.q: Why must a Merkle proof include the left/right position of each sibling?
quiz.a: H(a || b) ≠ H(b || a), so the verifier must join the running hash and sibling in the same order used to build the tree.

quiz.q: What does || mean in H(h<sub>1</sub> || h<sub>2</sub>)?
quiz.a: Concatenation: the bytes of h<sub>1</sub> followed by the bytes of h<sub>2</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Merkle trees also secure Git commits, Certificate Transparency logs and content-addressed stores such as IPFS. Ethereum's Patricia trie adds a radix structure so keys can be looked up, not only proved. Newer work uses Merkle Mountain Ranges for append-only logs. Search for Merkle proof, Certificate Transparency and Merkle Patricia trie to go further.
